name: NCAA.org Homepage, Official NCAA Athletics Website
title: NCAA.org Homepage, Official NCAA Athletics Website
answer: This source is the NCAA.org homepage, the official athletics website of the NCAA. It is a short landing page rather than a policy document. Its most useful statement for a reader is that the NCAA describes itself as serving 1,000+ member schools across all three divisions through dedicated governance, trusted standards and championships. The page does not mention artificial intelligence, recruiting analytics, roster management or transfer analytics. It offers only general background on the NCAA's role and no specific AI guidance.

sections.body: The NCAA publishes this page as its official athletics website, NCAA.org. It is a homepage or landing page, not a report or policy document. Its scope is the NCAA's support for student-athletes, member schools and championships across 1,000+ member schools and all three divisions. It also includes cookie and bot management notices. No publication date is stated in the text.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page identifies itself as the official athletics website of NCAA.org. It says the NCAA supports student-athletes, member schools and championships. Across 1,000+ member schools and all three divisions, it says the NCAA unlocks transformative opportunities and lifelong well-being for student-athletes. It states that college sports are the world's greatest tool for human development and that success is its purpose, in competition and beyond sports. It says NCAA staff and partners have helped today's student-athletes have more support, opportunity and resources than ever, and that this support goes beyond school and athletic environments. Through dedicated governance, trusted standards and championships, it says the NCAA is there for student-athletes and the schools that serve them. It notes that each division is special and invites readers to see what sets each apart. The rest of the text is cookie and bot management information. It describes cookies used to operate NCAA.org, improve site performance, understand visitor use and support digital communications. It mentions consent to privacy and cookie policies, managing preferences and opting out of non-essential cookies. It also describes Cloudflare bot products, the __cf_bm cookie, the cf_ob_info cookie and sequence cookies used to track request order and timing.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that the NCAA covers 1,000+ member schools and all three divisions. It says the NCAA offers dedicated governance, trusted standards and championships. It names three cookie or bot items: __cf_bm, which it says is necessary for proper functioning, cf_ob_info, which it says provides the HTTP Status Code, Ray ID and data center, and sequence cookies, which it says track request order and timing. The text gives no AI related numbers, definitions or policy positions.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in sports would find this source useful only as general background on the NCAA's stated role. It confirms the NCAA presents itself as the official athletics website for 1,000+ member schools across all three divisions and mentions dedicated governance and trusted standards. It does not discuss AI, recruiting, roster management, transfer analytics or any policy answers on those topics. Anyone looking for NCAA AI policy would need a different source. This page can serve as background on the organization, not as evidence of AI rules.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Sports

sections.body: The text is a homepage, not a policy document. It does not cover AI, recruiting, roster management or transfer analytics. It gives no publication date. It is high level and partial, with much of the text devoted to cookies and bot management. It does not provide governance details or standards.
